docs.title: PyconFR 2025 (30 October - 2 Novembre)
docs.text:
Greeting !!

It was a pleasure to attend PyconFR 2025 in Lyon. Overall, the atmosphere was perfect, and I had the chance to meet some great people (Geeks) from some companies like Redhat, Worteks, Elastic...

Pyconfr is an event organized by Afpy once a year, bringing together Python developers and anyone else who wants to discover Python.

I took part in a contribution session for Ansible, where the goal was to try to resolve an issue for any Ansible module. ansible-collections

The workshop was led by two people, @pilou and @mscherer. He's an idea of the program :

  • Correction of existing bugs.
  • Reviews of existing pull requests.
  • Correction of unstable tests.
  • Improvement of documentation.
  • Addition of unit tests (tox/mock) and integration tests (docker/lxc).

Another workshop I participated in was creating the CI/CD chain with Nox, and the main goal was to automate the development process with Python via Nox to create flexible test automation.

Nox is a tool designed to automate testing on multiple Python environments. It is similar to Tox. However, it uses the standard Python file for its configuration.

Here are the prerequisites for completing the exercises :

  • Laptop: Linux is highly recommended for this type of use, but Windows will also work if you have WSL & pyenv installed.
  • Git configured.
  • An account on GitHub or GitLab.
  • Basic knowledge of the command line (Linux).

The repository is available here : Gitlab-nox

Enjoyyyy :)

docs.title: Kind local kubernetes cluster
docs.text:
Kind (or Kubernetes in Docker) is one of the lightweight solutions for running your own Kubernetes cluster locally.

There are many ways to install Kind. In this guide, we’ll focus on the go install option. For other installation methods, refer to the Kind installation options.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Go 1.17 or later
  2. Docker or Podman
  3. kubectl

docs.title: Installing with go install
docs.text:
$ go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@v0.31.0

Note: When installing with Go, the Kind binary will be located in the bin directory under $(go env GOPATH). If you encounter the error kind: command not found, update your PATH environment variable.

docs.title: Creating a Cluster (Docker)
docs.text:
Ensure Docker is up and running.

Create a simple cluster configuration file. Here, we’ll specify the number of nodes:

kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

Create the cluster:

$ kind create cluster --name=coconut --config=kind-config.yaml

We use the --name and --config flags to override the default cluster name and specify a custom cluster configuration.

docs.title: Listing Clusters
docs.text:
$ kind get clusters
coconut

docs.title: Interacting with Your Cluster
docs.text:
$ kubectl cluster-info

Kubernetes control plane is running at https://127.0.0.1:44801
CoreDNS is running at https://127.0.0.1:44801/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/services/kube-dns:dns/proxy

To further debug and diagnose cluster problems, use 'kubectl cluster-info dump'.

docs.title: Deploy Your First App
docs.text: Once your cluster is up and running, let’s create a simple HTTP service and expose an Nginx server using an Ingress controller.

docs.title: 1. Check Node Status
docs.text:
$ kubectl get nodes

NAME                    STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
coconut-control-plane   Ready    control-plane   11m   v1.35.0
coconut-worker          Ready    <none>          10m   v1.35.0
coconut-worker2         Ready    <none>          10m   v1.35.0

docs.title: 2. Deploy the Nginx Ingress Controller
docs.text:
$ kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml

In this configuration, Ingress acts as the cluster’s reverse proxy and load balancer. For more details, see the Ingress documentation.

Wait for the Ingress controller pod to be running:

$ kubectl wait --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --for=condition=ready pod \
  --selector=app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx \
  --timeout=90s

Output:

pod/ingress-nginx-controller-56dc4b4c6-4622t condition met

docs.title: 3. Deploy Your Test Application
docs.text:
Create a YAML manifest for Pods, Services, and Ingress:

kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: foo-app
  labels:
    app: foo
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - /agnhost
    - serve-hostname
    - --http=true
    - --port=8080
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39
    name: foo-app
---
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: foo-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: foo
  ports:
  - port: 8080
---
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: bar-app
  labels:
    app: bar
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - /agnhost
    - serve-hostname
    - --http=true
    - --port=8080
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39
    name: bar-app
---
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: bar-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: bar
  ports:
  - port: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /foo
        backend:
          service:
            name: foo-service
            port:
              number: 8080
      - pathType: Prefix
        path: /bar
        backend:
          service:
            name: bar-service
            port:
              number: 8080

Apply the manifest:

$ kubectl apply -f echo-http.yaml

Verify the resources are created:

$ kubectl get pods,svc,ingress

docs.title: 4. Access Your Ingress Locally
docs.text:
Forward the Ingress controller’s port 80 to your local machine:

$ kubectl port-forward -n ingress-nginx service/ingress-nginx-controller 8080:80

Test your routes in a new terminal:

$ curl http://localhost:8080/foo
$ curl http://localhost:8080/bar

Expected output: The hostname of the foo-app or bar-app pod.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Check Ingress controller logs: 
    $ kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx
  • Check Ingress events: 
    $ kubectl describe ingress example-ingress
  • Verify services and pods: 
    $ kubectl get svc,ep

docs.title: Kubernetes by the hard way
docs.text:
This post is a short write-up of how I built a Kubernetes cluster by hand, following Kubernetes The Hard Way by Kelsey Hightower in its Rocky Linux adaptation by Wale Soyinka.

The Rocky Linux labs target Enterprise Linux on x86_64. I used Fedora Server 44 instead, with all the machines running as libvirt VMs on a single hypervisor that has only one public IP. Then I went further than the labs: cluster DNS, Argo CD, and public HTTPS access for apps.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: VM Role jumpbox Admin machine: kubectl, helm, certificates and configs server Control plane: etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler node-0, node-1 Workers: containerd, kubelet, kube-proxy Network Range Pod network node-0 10.200.0.0/24 Pod network node-1 10.200.1.0/24 Services 10.32.0.0/24 (API 10.32.0.1, DNS 10.32.0.10)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A host running Fedora Server with virtualization enabled
  2. libvirt with virt-install and virsh
  3. A Fedora Server 44 install image for the VMs
  4. Optional, for public access: a domain name pointing to the hypervisor's public IP

Install the virtualization stack on the host:

$ sudo dnf install -y @virtualization
$ sudo systemctl enable --now libvirtd

I created four VMs on the default libvirt NAT network. An example for one machine (adapt CPU, memory, disk and image path):

$ sudo virt-install \
    --name node-0 \
    --vcpus 2 --memory 4096 \
    --disk size=20 \
    --os-variant fedora-44 \
    --network network=default \
    --location /var/lib/libvirt/images/Fedora-Server-dvd-x86_64-44.iso \
    --graphics none --extra-args 'console=ttyS0'

Once all four are installed:

$ sudo virsh list --all
 Id   Name      State
-------------------------
 2    server    running
 3    jumpbox   running
 4    node-0    running
 5    node-1    running

docs.title: Following the labs
docs.text:
I followed the Rocky Linux labs in order. Most commands work unchanged on Fedora since both use dnf, systemd and NetworkManager.

  1. Prerequisites
  2. Set Up The Jumpbox
  3. Provisioning Compute Resources
  4. Provisioning a CA and Generating TLS Certificates
  5. Generating Kubernetes Configuration Files for Authentication
  6. Generating the Data Encryption Configuration and Key
  7. Bootstrapping the etcd Cluster
  8. Bootstrapping the Kubernetes Control Plane
  9. Bootstrapping the Kubernetes Worker Nodes
  10. Configuring kubectl for Remote Access
  11. Provisioning Pod Network Routes
  12. Smoke Test

At the end the smoke test passes: deployments, port-forward, logs, exec and NodePort services all work. But the cluster is still bare, and a few things bit me as soon as I tried to install a real application.

docs.title: Lesson 1: check the pod routes on every machine
docs.text:
Lab 11 adds static routes so each machine can reach the other workers' pods. Mine were incomplete: server only had a route to node-0's pods, and the two workers had no route to each other. The smoke test doesn't catch this because it only uses one pod.

Every machine needs a route to every other worker's pod network:

$ ssh root@server 'ip route | grep 10.200'
10.200.0.0/24 via <node-0 IP> dev enp1s0
10.200.1.0/24 via <node-1 IP> dev enp1s0

$ ssh root@node-0 'ip route | grep 10.200'
10.200.0.0/24 dev cni0 proto kernel scope link src 10.200.0.1
10.200.1.0/24 via <node-1 IP> dev enp1s0

ip route add is lost at reboot. On Fedora, make sure the routes are permanent with NetworkManager:

$ nmcli -g NAME,DEVICE con show --active
$ sudo nmcli con modify '<connection>' +ipv4.routes '10.200.1.0/24 <node-1 IP>'
$ sudo nmcli con up '<connection>'

Note: A missing route shows up later as random timeouts: DNS that works on one node only, webhooks that time out, certificates that never get issued. Check routes first.

docs.title: Lesson 2: the cluster has no DNS
docs.text:
The labs don't install a DNS add-on, so pods can't resolve service names. Almost every real app needs it :( . I installed CoreDNS with Helm from the jumpbox, on the IP the kubelets give pods as their DNS server (clusterDNS in the kubelet config):

$ ssh root@node-0 grep -A1 clusterDNS /var/lib/kubelet/kubelet-config.yaml

The first attempt crash-looped with plugin/loop: Loop ... detected: and the nodes /etc/resolv.conf points to a local resolver, so CoreDNS was forwarding queries to itself. The fix is to give it real upstream servers in a values file, coredns-values.yaml:

replicaCount: 2
service:
  clusterIP: 10.32.0.10
servers:
- zones:
  - zone: .
    use_tcp: true
  port: 53
  plugins:
  - name: errors
  - name: health
    configBlock: |-
      lameduck 10s
  - name: ready
  - name: kubernetes
    parameters: cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
    configBlock: |-
      pods insecure
      fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
      ttl 30
  - name: prometheus
    parameters: 0.0.0.0:9153
  - name: forward
    parameters: . 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8
  - name: cache
    parameters: 30
  - name: loop
  - name: reload
  - name: loadbalance

$ helm repo add coredns https://coredns.github.io/helm
$ helm upgrade --install coredns coredns/coredns -n kube-system -f coredns-values.yaml

Test from a pod:

$ kubectl run dnstest --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
    sh -c 'nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local; nslookup github.com'

docs.title: Lesson 3: the control plane can't reach Services
docs.text:
The server machine runs no kube-proxy, so the API server can't reach Service IPs. That breaks anything with an admission webhook, such as cert-manager (failed calling webhook ... context deadline exceeded).

The fix is one flag in /etc/systemd/system/kube-apiserver.service on server, which makes the API server call webhook pods by their pod IPs (reachable thanks to the routes from lesson 1):

  --enable-aggregator-routing=true \

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kube-apiserver

docs.title: Deploying Argo CD
docs.text:
Argo CD runs fine on this cluster once DNS works. It needs no persistent storage.

$ kubectl create namespace argocd
$ kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts \
    -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
$ kubectl -n argocd get pods -w

Get the initial admin password:

$ kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
    -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo

docs.title: Exposing apps with a single public ip
docs.text:
Only the hypervisor is reachable from the internet, and there is no cloud LoadBalancer. My setup :"

  • Traefik as ingress controller, exposed as a NodePort on 30080 / 30443.
  • HAProxy on the hypervisor, passing TCP 80 / 443 to those nodeports.
  • cert-manager with let's encrypt for TLS.

  • One DNS record per app pointing to the public ip .

  • Traefik

$ helm repo add traefik https://traefik.github.io/charts
$ helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace \
    --set service.type=NodePort \
    --set ports.web.nodePort=30080 \
    --set ports.websecure.nodePort=30443 \
    --set deployment.replicas=2 \
    --set ingressClass.isDefaultClass=true
  1. HAproxy (on the hypervisor)

Added to /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg 

frontend http_in
    bind *:80
    mode tcp
    default_backend k8s_http

frontend https_in
    bind *:443
    mode tcp
    default_backend k8s_https

backend k8s_http
    mode tcp
    balance roundrobin
    server node0 <node-0 IP>:30080 check
    server node1 <node-1 IP>:30080 check

backend k8s_https
    mode tcp
    balance roundrobin
    server node0 <node-0 IP>:30443 check
    server node1 <node-1 IP>:30443 check


$ sudo setsebool -P haproxy_connect_any 1
$ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
$ sudo firewall-cmd --reload
$ sudo systemctl enable --now haproxy
  1. cert-manager and let's encryt
$ sudo setsebool -P haproxy_connect_any 1
$ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
$ sudo firewall-cmd --reload
$ sudo systemctl enable --now haproxy

issuers.yaml : 

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: <your email>
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: traefik
  1. ArgoCD over HTTPS

Traefik terminates TLS, so ArgoCD serves plain HTTP behind it: 

$ kubectl -n argocd patch configmap argocd-cmd-params-cm --type merge \
    -p '{"data":{"server.insecure":"true"}}'
$ kubectl -n argocd rollout restart deployment argocd-server

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: argocd-server
  namespace: argocd
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  tls:
    - hosts: [argocd.<your-domain>]
      secretName: argocd-server-tls
  rules:
    - host: argocd.<your-domain>
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: argocd-server
                port:
                  number: 80

$ kubectl get certificate -n argocd
$ argocd login argocd.<your-domain> --grpc-web --username admin

Argo CD is now reachable at https://argocd. with a valid certificate.

docs.title: Vagrant getting started
docs.text:
“Vagrant is a versatile tool used by devops engineers, developers, system administrators, and tech enthusiasts to create development and testing environments. It enables building and managing virtual machines within a single streamlined workflow. By focusing on automation, it reduces environment setup time, and makes the works on my machine issue a thing of the past.”

If you’re already comfortable with Vagrant basics, the official documentation serves as a thorough reference for all features.

Vagrant provides easy to configure, reproducible, and portable environments built on industry-standard technology and controlled by one consistent workflow. This helps to maximize the productivity and flexibility of you and your team.

https://developer.hashicorp.com/vagrant/intro

This guide explains how to get Vagrant running on fedora based system. I started with minimal Fedora install to minimize the host’s memory footprint, but the steps should work on any Fedora setup, whether Server or Workstation.

  1. Verify the machine supports wirtualisation: 

    $ sudo lscpu | grep Virtualization
Virtualization:                  VT-x
Virtualization type:             full

  2. Install qemu-kvm: 

    $ sudo dnf install qemu-kvm libvirt libguestfs-tools virt-install rsync

  3. Start and enable libvirt daemon: 

    $ sudo systemctl enable --now libvirtd

  4. Install Vagrant: 

    $ sudo dnf install vagrant

  5. Install libvirtd’s plugin: 

    $ sudo vagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt

  6. Add the box: 

    $ vagrant box add fedora/41-cloud-base --provider=libvirt

  7. Set up environment: 

    $ mkdir vagrant-demo
$ cd vagrant-demo
$ vi Vagrantfile
Vagrant.configure("2") do |config|
  config.vm.box = "fedora/41-cloud-base"
end

  8. Check the file: 

    $ vagrant status
Current machine states:

default not created (libvirt)

The Libvirt domain is not created. Run 'vagrant up' to create it.

  9. Start the box: 

    $ vagrant up

  10. Connect to your machine: 

    $ vagrant ssh

Yeahhh, that’s it, you’ve now Vagrant working on you machine.

“To stop the machine”, use vagrant halt, it simply halts the host, leaving the vm and its storage disk in place.

Tips: There’s no need to download boxes ahead of time, you can define the box provider in the Vagrantfile, then Vagrant will download the box when you run vagrant up if it’s missing. The following example includes Memory and CPU configuration: 

# -*- mode: ruby -*-
# vi: set ft=ruby :

Vagrant.configure("2") do |config|
  config.vm.box = "fedora/41-cloud-base"
  config.vm.provider :libvirt do |libvirt|
    libvirt.cpus = 1
    libvirt.memory = 1024
  end
end

For more details on using Vagrant, creating own machines, and working with different boxes, refer to the official documentation at https://www.vagrantup.com/docs
